claims: Colon cancer develops from polyps in the colon or rectum.
Colon cancer primarily affects adults over 45.
Incidence of colon cancer is rising in younger people.
Early-stage colon cancer is often asymptomatic.
Diarrhea that does not go away is a symptom of colon cancer.
Constipation that does not go away is a symptom of colon cancer.
Narrowing of the stool that does not go away is a symptom of colon cancer.
Blood in the stool is a symptom of colon cancer.
Bright red blood from the rectum is a symptom of colon cancer.
Frequent gas pains are a symptom of colon cancer.
Bloating is a symptom of colon cancer.
Fullness is a symptom of colon cancer.
Cramps are a symptom of colon cancer.
Unexplained weight loss is a symptom of colon cancer.
Feeling consistently tired is a symptom of colon cancer.
Iron-deficiency anemia is a symptom of colon cancer.
Risk of colon cancer increases with age, particularly over 50.
Cases of colon cancer are rising in those under 50.
A history of colorectal polyps increases the risk of colon cancer.
A history of colorectal cancer increases the risk of colon cancer.
A history of ulcerative colitis increases the risk of colon cancer.
A history of Crohn's disease increases the risk of colon cancer.
Diets high in red or processed meats increase the risk of colon cancer.
Sedentary lifestyle increases the risk of colon cancer.
Obesity increases the risk of colon cancer.
Smoking increases the risk of colon cancer.
Heavy alcohol use increases the risk of colon cancer.
Inherited syndromes such as Lynch syndrome increase the risk of colon cancer.
Colon cancer is classified using the TNM staging system.
Stage 0 colon cancer is carcinoma in situ on the innermost layer of the colon.
Stage I/II colon cancer has grown deeper into the wall of the colon but has not spread to lymph nodes or other organs.
Stage III colon cancer has spread to nearby lymph nodes.
Stage IV colon cancer has spread to other parts of the body, such as the liver or lungs.
The five-year survival rate for stages I and II colon cancer is approximately 91%.
The five-year survival rate for stage IV colon cancer is approximately 13%.
Regular screenings such as colonoscopies starting at age 45 can detect precancerous polyps.
Regular screenings can remove precancerous polyps.
Primary treatment for colon cancer is often surgery.
Colon cancer treatment is sometimes combined with chemotherapy.
Colon cancer treatment is sometimes combined with radiation.
Colon cancer treatment is sometimes combined with targeted therapies.
